sections.html:
• Name: Emerald crab
  • Other names: Emerald Mythrax Crab, Green Crab, Green Clinging Crab, Jade crab
  • Scientific name: Mithraculus sculptus
  • Minimum tank size: 40 litres
  • Breeding: Very difficult
  • Water: SG 1.023–1.025
  • KH: 8–12
  • Nitrate: less than 20 ppm
  • Diet: Omnivore
  • Temperament (reef safe): considered safe, may be aggressive
  • Life span: up to 4 years
  • Colour: green
These crabs are abundant in shallow waters of the tropical western Atlantic Ocean, from as far north as Miami, throughout the Bahamas and Caribbean, and south to northern Brazil.
They are common in reefs, living in rock cavities, corals or sponges from intertidal to a maximum 55 m depth.

Minimum tank size is 40 litres. Do not keep more than 1 crab per 40 litres, else it can lead to aggression amongst themselves. In most cases, there is no need to have more than one in your tank at a time. In a small tank, it is better to have only one crab or a pair of the opposite sex.

Emerald crabs are very popular also because of their hardiness. They only require an established aquarium with plenty of live rock and reef work for hiding places and to scavenge for algae, but are otherwise undemanding and very easy to maintain.

Be careful with chemicals like copper. Crabs, shrimp, and crayfish do not tolerate copper-based medications or fluctuating water parameters.

Acclimatize them before putting them into the tank, otherwise you run a higher risk of your crabs dying because of shock.

Like all crustaceans, they need to molt to grow. Once the outer shell is shed, it is common to think that the crab is dead, but it isn't. During this time the crab hides in the rocks or crevices until the new shell becomes hard. Do not throw away old shells: they contain lots of minerals and crabs will gladly eat them after some time. The molting frequency, growth, and survival of crustaceans depend on diet, temperature, and water quality.
Emerald crabs thrive when the water temperature is kept between 24–28°C, pH 8.0–8.4, KH 8–12, and SG 1.023–1.025. Nitrate should be less than 20 ppm.

Emerald crabs are not fussy eaters. Although often sold as herbivores, they are actually omnivorous. They will eat leftover meaty foods and algae that grow naturally in the tank. Mithraculus have modified, spoon-shaped claws to feed on both fleshy and filamentous algae, but they may consume alternative foods offered in a reef aquarium.

If an Emerald crab is not given a supplemental diet, it may start to mess with corals and prey on smaller fish, shrimp or crabs in the same tank. Well-fed crabs can become very tolerant of tank mates, so some aquarists supplement their diet about 2–3 times a week. Mysis shrimp does not affect their appetite, and krill probably will not either. Be very careful with any algae products.

In a study, Emerald crabs preferred pellets to Bubble algae. Algal consumption was similar when mysids were provided. Small crabs consumed significantly less than medium and large crabs, which did not differ significantly from each other. Smaller crabs were better at controlling algae in hard-to-access areas such as crevices.

When the crab tears the algal cell apart, cell liquid containing juvenile cytoplasmatic spheres is released into the water, which might contribute to algal dispersal. To avoid that, the crab's consumption rate must be higher than the growth of the Bubble algae, so one crab may not be able to clean a huge, heavily infested tank.

Both in the wild and in captivity, Emerald crabs are nocturnal, so provide proper rocks and stones where they can hide in dark corners and crevices. Once adapted to a tank, they may come out during the day.

They can be aggressive to each other. Their aggression towards other animals is debated: some aquarists report no problems, while others report them picking at SPS corals, mushrooms, zoas and sponges. Like most crabs, they are opportunistic, and their tendencies depend on food availability.

  • Keep an eye on it for the first week or so.
  • Do not let it get hungry.
  • Choose females. They are smaller and less aggressive.
  • Provide lots of hiding places.
  • The bigger the tank, the better.

Small crabs can be kept with small, non-aggressive, top or mid-dwelling fish. Avoid bottom fish, which the crab can injure with its claws. Very large fish may prey on the crab. Hermit crabs and snails are always at risk as they move slowly. Shrimp are too fast but can occasionally be eaten.

Flip the crab over and look at the underside. In males, the pleon (abdomen, the part folded underneath the crab) is narrower and in females it is wider and rounder. Males are also a little bigger and have larger claws than females.

Breeding is not known in detail, and no systematic breeding protocol exists.

Females can produce from several dozen (usually a few hundred) to 1000 eggs per spawn. The eggs are carried under the female's abdomen for a few weeks, after which the larvae are released. Larval development consists of two zoeal stages (about 2 days each) and one megalopa stage (3 to 9 days). Overall survival in experiments was lower than 10–20%.

Larvae need newly hatched or enriched Artemia nauplii right after hatching; starved larvae fail to develop past zoea 1. The best result was at 7–15 nauplii per mL.

  • Salinity 35
  • Temperature 28–29°C
  • pH 8.0–8.2
  • Photoperiod 14 h light / 10 h dark
  • Ammonia, nitrite and nitrate below detectable levels

A cylindrical tank reduces larval collisions with the walls. Avoid rocks in the rearing setup. Post-larval crabs are aggressive and kill each other until only one remains.

Emerald crabs are probably the most heavily traded crab in the marine aquarium industry and are used to control nuisance algae, particularly Bubble algae (Valonia spp.). The marine ornamental industry relies heavily on wild-collected specimens, mainly from coral reefs.
